comments: Struck in the head and neck area with a heavy box. May have lost consciousness briefly. Suffered pain in her neck, shoulder, upper body, and chest. Sustained a major injury to her cervical spine causing her pre-existing spinal condition to become symptomatic. The injury also resulted in spinal cord compression in plaintiff's neck, resulting in permanent effects on her spinal nerves, causing slight weakness of the left upper limb and slight sensory symptoms in the left side of her body. P’s testimony was not credible at times.

comments: Plaintiff (Mary) was driving car with her husband seated next to her and three sons belted in the back seat.  The car was struck by defendant who went through a red light.  The violent collision injured the plaintiff and her two sons and killed the youngest son.  The plaintiff suffered soft tissue injuries to her neck, left leg and lower back, headaches, pain in her back and her leg, fractures to her lumber spine.  She was left with ongoing back pain that limited all areas of her life.  In addition, she suffered mental and emotional distress as a result of the death of her son that would last her entire life. Plaintiff had a moderately impaired cognitive status after the collision, with the impairment resulting from the brain injury, chronic pain, and depression. Plaintiff has been unable to finish high school,.

Deductions from the damage award will only be given if absolutely clear that benefits are certain to be received.  There is a “strict onus of proof” and “patently clear” that preconditions for an appropriate deduction have been established.  It is uncertain if plaintiff will receive benefits. Motion dismissed.

P testified that the upset from the injury caused sufficient strain on his marriage that he eventually separated from his wife and daughter and was unable to return to his employment, and as a result closed the store he owned with financial loss.

comments: Missed diagnosis of appendicitis and peritonitis and after effects including  severe untreated pain over several days leading up to the rupture of appendix ; the trauma of life-threatening peritonitis and an emergency appendectomy; the painful and debilitating after-effects of all the related surgeries and convalescences; the uncertainty between as to whether a satisfactory fusion of his incision would ever be achieved: and the frustration and anxiety resulting from the adverse effects of all of the above on his career and personal relationships; scarring materially contributed to clinical depression from which he continues to suffer.

Profound grief since losing his partner of over 10 years, with three children under 8. ncontested evidence of negative affects on the children.

comments: MVA-The plaintiff suffered catastrophic injuries when his tow truck was rear-ended by the defendant. Prejudgment interest on general damage award was calculated at 5%, plaintiff was required to assign his future income replacement benefit from his SABs insurer only to the age of 60, jury should treat Ontario Drug Benefit Program as contingency only, rather than as certainty, and there should be no assignment to defendant of future payments to be made to plaintiff by SABS insurer for medication, assistive devices and services. Defendant’s appeal allowed. 2017 September 19 [2017] O.J. No. 4828 ONCA D.H. Doherty, J.L. MacFarland and P.S. Rouleau JJ.A. On appeal: interest award adjusted to $44,583.90 (2.5% interest rate (Appeal allowed:  (a)  The judgment was reduced by the sum of $44,583.90 to reflect an interest rate of 2.5% on the general damage award.  (b)  The obligation to assign the income replacement benefits payable by RSA Insurance should continue until the respondant’s 64th birthday.  (c)  The trial judge erred in in failing to instruct jury not to award any sum for drug benefits after plaintiff reached age of 65 because from that age forward, he would suffer no loss because his drug claims would be covered by Ontario Drug Benefit Program. d)  The trial judge erred in not ordering an assignment in relation to the awards for the cost of future medication and assistive devices and future professional services.

comments: P  A  PPlaintiff was wrongfully dismissed because of hearing loss.  Plaintiff suffers from adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed moods caused by the manner of dismissal.  laintiff appealed the motion judge’s assessment of damages and costs. Damages were increased accordingly.   General damages: The court determined that the motion judge failed to consider the increased costs of therapy resulting from the plaintiff’s permanent deafness. unitive damages: The motion judge erred in finding that the defendant’s failure to profit from the misconduct mitigated their level of blameworthiness. ggravated damages:  The motion judge erred in finding a complete overlap between this head of damages and those awarded for wrongful dismissal.
